Companion Creatures.name: Companion Creatures
Companion Creatures.text:
Characters can acquire companion creatures by a variety of means. Some can be purchased from merchants for a few Gold Pieces, sometimes with a minimum renown threshold. Others are found as treasure, given as rewards for completing an adventure, or even found while using gathering professions. (For example, mining elementium in level 17+ zones can sometimes release an elementium geode, a kind of elemental companion.)

Companion creatures are too small to serve as mounts, too weak to participate meaningfully in combat, and generally incapable of useful independent action. Much like mounts, though, they can serve as badges of honor, marking a character’s achievements or the breadth of their travels.

Calling a Companion.name: Calling a Companion
Calling a Companion.text:
Companion creatures are magically bound to a character. Some appear when summoned and disappear to some other plane when dismissed. Others are natural creatures bound to magical items (often collars or leashes) that allow a character to summon and dismiss them in the same way. Still others are mechanical or magical constructs that can be deactivated, rather than dismissed, and stored with the character’s gear. In any case, summoning or dismissing a companion requires the character to take the Magic action, and a character can have only one companion summoned in this way at a time. Summoning a new companion instantly dismisses a companion that is already present. While summoned, a companion stays within 5 feet of the character by floating or flying nearby, perching on the character’s shoulder, or following on foot.

A companion creature can’t take actions and can’t be targeted by attacks. If it takes any damage (for example, if the character is caught in a @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.spells.Item.phbsplFireball00]{Fireball} spell’s area), it is instantly dismissed or deactivated.

Companion Loyalty.name: Companion Loyalty
Companion Loyalty.text:
A companion creature has a Loyalty Score, using @UUID[Compendium.dnd-dungeon-masters-guide.content.JournalEntry.dmgDmsToolbox000.JournalEntryPage.xO6TMYeaWvBtj0RV]{the rules} in the Dungeon Master’s Guide, but its loyalty is to an individual and not to the party. When a character acquires a companion, the companion’s Loyalty Score equals the character’s Charisma modifier (minimum of 1). The companion’s Loyalty Score can’t be higher than the character’s Charisma.

A companion creature’s Loyalty Score increases by [[/r 1d4]] if the companion is treated particularly well, which might include buying special food for it, pampering it in other ways, or rescuing it from danger. Its Loyalty Score decreases by 1 if it is dismissed or deactivated by taking damage.

If a companion creature’s Loyalty Score reaches 10 or higher, the companion gives the character a small supernatural gift while the companion is present. The nature of this gift depends on the companion’s category, as described below.

Types of Companions.name: Types of Companions
Types of Companions.text:
The following sections detail different types of companions characters might discover.

Aquatic Companions

Aquatic companion creatures include fish, crabs, frogs, octopi, water birds, turtles, otters, and other water-dwelling creatures. Sometimes they float in a bubble of water near their owners.

While you have an aquatic companion whose Loyalty Score is 10 or higher, you have the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.items.Item.wowAquaticCompan]{Blessing of the Aquatic Companion}, which gives you a Swim Speed equal to your Speed.

Beast Companions

Beast companion creatures are natural animals that neither fly nor swim. They include Tiny and Small beasts, as well as the young of larger creatures. (These beasts don’t age while kept as a companion.)

While you have a beast companion whose Loyalty Score is 10 or higher, you have the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.items.Item.wowBeastCompanio]{Blessing of the Beast Companion}, which gives you proficiency and Expertise in Animal Handling and Survival.

Dragonkin Companions

Dragonkin companion creatures include dragon whelplings—younger and smaller than the whelps described in @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze]{chapter 7}—as well as draconic animals native to the Dragon Isles.

While you have a dragonkin companion whose Loyalty Score is 10 or higher, you have the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.items.Item.wowDragonkinComp]{Blessing of the Dragonkin Companion}, which gives you Advantage on saving throws to avoid or end the Frightened condition.

Elemental Companions

Elemental companion creatures include animate plants and remnants of the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowConflictsOfAz.JournalEntryPage.QX2LRHkL98AMmC55]{Old Gods}’ power as well as living motes of elemental energy.

While you have an elemental companion whose Loyalty Score is 10 or higher, you have the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.items.Item.wowElementalComp]{Blessing of the Elemental Companion}, which gives you Advantage on saving throws to avoid or end the Exhaustion condition.

Flying Companions

Flying companions include flying creatures—ordinary birds, bats, moths, bumblebees, and flying snakes—and magical versions of these creatures.

While you have a flying companion whose Loyalty Score is 10 or higher, you have the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.items.Item.wowFlyingCompani]{Blessing of the Flying Companion}, which increases your Speed by 5 feet.

Humanoid Companions

Humanoid companions include imps, kobolds, baby murlocs, and a range of other beings that can help you in ways that don’t involve combat. The DM is encouraged to develop any humanoid companion as an NPC using @UUID[Compendium.dnd-dungeon-masters-guide.content.JournalEntry.dmgDmsToolbox000.JournalEntryPage.5GOEEHaai1dsSxbx]{the guidelines} in the Dungeon Master’s Guide.

While you have a humanoid companion whose Loyalty Score is 10 or higher, you have the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.items.Item.wowHumanoidCompa]{Blessing of the Humanoid Companion}, which gives you proficiency and Expertise in the Persuasion skill.

Magic Companions

Magic companions encompass a variety of beings that are fundamentally magical, including tiny fragments of Old Gods or other powers, stray eyes or tentacles of otherworldly origin, oozes, creatures of the Void, ghostly spirits, and animated magical tomes.

While you have a magic companion whose Loyalty Score is 10 or higher, you have the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.items.Item.wowMagicCompanio]{Blessing of the Magic Companion}, which gives you proficiency and Expertise in the Arcana skill.

Mechanical Companions

Mechanical companions are clockwork or otherwise engineered creatures, ranging from mechanical chickens to diminutive replicas of the Burning Legion’s terrifying fel reaver constructs.

While you have a mechanical companion whose Loyalty Score is 10 or higher, you have the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.items.Item.wowMechanicalCom]{Blessing of the Mechanical Companion}, which allows you to roll [[/r 1d4]] whenever you take Psychic damage and reduce the damage taken by the number rolled.

Undead Companions

Undead companions include skeletal or ghostly animals and similar creatures.

While you have an undead companion whose Loyalty Score is 10 or higher, you have the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.items.Item.wowUndeadCompani]{Blessing of the Undead Companion}, which gives you Advantage on Death Saving Throws.

Overview.name: Overview
Overview.text:
As described in the Dungeon Master’s Guide, a helpful way to think about a campaign setting is to @UUID[Compendium.dnd-dungeon-masters-guide.content.JournalEntry.dmgCampaignPremi.JournalEntryPage.IzpMNawOjfqvswS9]{outline the conflicts} that drive adventures in that world. Six interrelated conflicts have driven the action of the World of Warcraft game:

  • @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowTheAlliance00]{Alliance} versus @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowTheHorde00000]{Horde}

  • Sargeras and the @UUID[.mOeoKWAu3OOx8LP9]{Burning Legion}

  • The @UUID[.2MFeGdKlqPZz0K4s]{dragonflights}

  • The @UUID[.DUxMQYjqDUIm5sGd]{elemental lords}

  • The @UUID[.QX2LRHkL98AMmC55]{Old Gods} and void lords

  • The @UUID[.YRwQ3wrLM22odUUP]{Scourge}

A D&D campaign in Azeroth might focus on only three of these, as the Dungeon Master’s Guide suggests, or might shift conflicts in and out of the spotlight as the characters advance in level. This section describes each of these conflicts, including sketches of how they might manifest during each tier of play. Unlike the conflict arcs in the Dungeon Master’s Guide, those described here include suggestions for “endgame” play—continuing play with the characters at level 20, gaining @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.content.JournalEntry.phbFeats00000000.JournalEntryPage.GxfrwkJbrIvn7reC]{bonus feats} as described in the Player’s Handbook.

Alliance and Horde.name: Alliance and Horde
Alliance and Horde.text:
The hostilities between @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowTheAlliance00]{the Alliance} and @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowTheHorde00000]{the Horde} are a central conflict of the Warcraft setting. Ever since orcs first came through the Dark Portal from Draenor to Azeroth and waged war against the humans of the Eastern Kingdoms, the Alliance and the Horde have sought each other’s destruction or at least submission. Though other conflicts have forced the Alliance and the Horde to cooperate to repel greater threats, such truces are uneasy. To date, the longest has lasted eight years and still holds, though many wonder how much longer the peace can continue.

You can approach this conflict in a couple of ways. In the first, the characters belong to a single faction, either Alliance or Horde, and their adventures bring them into conflict with the champions and armies of the other side. This approach fits a campaign set between the opening of the Dark Portal and the end of the Fourth War, some thirty-five years later.

In the other approach, the adventurers might include characters aligned with both factions, and the conflict between the factions is an obstacle they must overcome—perhaps in the name of peace or as a means to overcome a greater threat, such as another conflict discussed in this chapter.

With this approach, the Alliance–Horde conflict doesn’t have a campaign arc; rather, it complicates other arcs you’re using. At every tier of play, introduce scenarios where the characters have to overcome tension, disagreements, or violence between the Alliance and the Horde so the factions can achieve peace or deal with the other threat.

An Alliance–Horde Arc

The conflict between the Alliance and the Horde might play out in a campaign according to this broad outline. This outline assumes that the characters have aligned themselves with one faction.

Levels 1–4. While engaged in other adventures, low-level characters might encounter the opposing faction. For example, when Alliance characters enter the Stormwind Stockade, they might find a prominent Horde leader being held prisoner. Or Horde characters exploring Ragefire Chasm might discover lost SI:7 agents sent by the Alliance. Alternatively, the characters might travel through areas where the Alliance and the Horde are skirmishing.

Levels 5–10. The characters get drawn into battle against the opposing faction. For these scenarios, you can find abundant inspiration from PvP battlegrounds in World of Warcraft. For example, the characters might be recruited to fight the other faction in Warsong Gulch or the Arathi Basin. In addition to battling rank-and-file soldiers of the opposing faction, the characters also encounter adventurers of a skill level similar to their own. Any NPC adventurers who survive these battles might become recurring opponents in the campaign.

Levels 11–16. As the characters reach higher levels, they might be drawn into more significant conflicts against the opposing faction. You might have the characters be among the first outsiders to visit Pandaria, setting off a rivalry with the opposing faction (whether or not that rivalry is fueled by the increasingly outrageous plans of Horde Warchief Garrosh Hellscream, as it was in the Mists of Pandaria expansion). Alternatively, the characters could find themselves in the midst of the Fourth War (the time of the Battle for Azeroth expansion), undertaking island expeditions and advancing the war campaign for their faction.

Levels 17–20. The characters are viewed as the champions of their faction by others—including the champions of the opposing faction—making the characters a target. The characters might strive for leadership of their faction, try to overthrow the leadership of the opposing faction, or pursue peace between the factions. Alternatively, the faction conflict could complicate another conflict; for example, the characters might battle the opposing faction in Winterspring to claim powerful artifacts for their faction to use against the Lich King.

Endgame. After the characters reach level 20, they are likely to join forces with the opposing faction to counter one of the world-threatening dangers described later in this chapter. They might need to set aside grudges against recurring champions of the opposing faction who have caused them much distress.

Burning Legion.name: Burning Legion
Burning Legion.text:
@Embed[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowArtHandouts00.JournalEntryPage.avSYGRHj7B8bGeSY classes="noborder"]

The Burning Legion is one of the most destructive forces in the physical universe. The fallen titan Sargeras created this vast demonic army to scour all creation. The Burning Legion moves from world to world, destroying everything in its path with devastating fel magic. No one knows exactly how many worlds and mortal civilizations the demons have annihilated in their unholy Burning Crusade.

The demons that make up the Burning Legion include creatures drawn from the many worlds the Legion has conquered. Sargeras corrupted two of the three leaders of the eredar people of Argus—Archimonde and Kil’jaeden—turning them and their people into demonic beings. (The third leader, Prophet Velen, still leads the uncorrupted eredar, now called draenei.) Archimonde empowered the monstrous pit lords and conscripted them to serve as living siege engines. Kil’jaeden brought in devious succubi and incubi (collectively called sayaad) to infiltrate prospective worlds for conquest and gather intelligence about their civilizations. The brutal doomguard, demon warriors of unsurpassed strength and cruelty, fought as the Legion’s shock troops. The zealous shivarra became the Legion’s foremost mystics and advisers, fostering a fanatical loyalty to Sargeras. These wicked creatures, among many others, bolstered the might of the Burning Legion. For more on agents of the Legion such as @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze.JournalEntryPage.m7WElR3fFm7BX6eS]{doomguard}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze.JournalEntryPage.y718rEJ1hNCYH7RD]{felguard}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze.JournalEntryPage.Xkd9lZp4CbeapZ09]{felhounds}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze.JournalEntryPage.xcfzaJ68hbjOiYth]{infernals}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze.JournalEntryPage.dlCTexYw9RGffGaI]{pit lords}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze.JournalEntryPage.4yblb5rRbngox4cD]{satyrs}, and @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze.JournalEntryPage.CtFcEjVi6u59fwby]{shivarra}, see chapter 7. @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.content.JournalEntry.mmMonstersAtoZ00.JournalEntryPage.nM9DcYQzVicWFffF]{Succubi} and @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.content.JournalEntry.mmMonstersAtoZ00.JournalEntryPage.a5EpOcLCNws9jXXz]{incubi} (see the Monster Manual) also serve the Legion.

The Burning Legion has invaded Azeroth three times. In the War of the Ancients, ten thousand years ago, the Legion’s invasion led to the Great Sundering that shaped the world. The Legion corrupted the orcs of Draenor and sent them through the Dark Portal, beginning the First War. The @UUID[.YRwQ3wrLM22odUUP]{Scourge} has its origins in the fel magic of the Burning Legion, and the Scourge’s advance in the Third War paved the way for the Burning Legion to enter the world a second time. Years later, a new portal allowed the Legion access to Azeroth—but the heroes of Azeroth took the fight to Argus and defeated the Legion there.

Goals of the Burning Legion

Sargeras formed the Burning Legion because he believed creation was fatally flawed. The presence of the void lords corrupting Worldsouls across the universe (see @UUID[.QX2LRHkL98AMmC55]{Old Gods} below) was a prospect that terrified the titan. This threat ultimately convinced him that the only way to spare the universe from the potential of a Void-corrupted titan was to purge all creation in fire and begin again from the ashes. So he released the demons he had previously banished to a pocket dimension and formed them into his agents of apocalypse.

Sargeras and his lieutenants have a particular grudge against Azeroth, the only world they have failed to conquer—not once, but multiple times. The power of Azeroth’s Worldsoul is undeniable, which makes it (in Sargeras’s mind) that much more important that it be destroyed before it can be corrupted into an unstoppable void titan.

A Burning Legion Arc

A campaign featuring the Burning Legion might unfold according to this outline.

Levels 1–4. Early in their adventuring careers, characters might encounter the fringes of the Burning Legion, such as satyrs in northern Kalimdor or one of the cults serving the Burning Legion (for example, the Cult of the Dark Strand in Darkshore, the Veiled Hand in Duskwood, or the Burning Blade in Durotar). These encounters can be an opportunity for characters to learn about the history of the Legion’s interference on Azeroth.

The characters might aid Sentinel Elissa Starbreeze in Auberdine (in Darkshore), Delgren the Purifier in Maestra’s Post (in Ashenvale), and Delgren’s agent Balthule Shadowstrike, who are investigating the Cult of the Dark Strand along Kalimdor’s northwestern coast. That investigation culminates in the Tower of Althalaxx in northern Darkshore. Alternatively, characters might join a similar investigation into the Burning Blade cultists residing atop Dreadmist Peak in the Barrens.

Levels 5–10. Having defeated one small cult, the characters discover that such cults are only parts of a much larger effort by a group called the Shadow Council to advance the power of the Burning Legion on Azeroth. The characters might confront lesser demons of the Legion in Demon Fall Canyon or Felfire Hill in Ashenvale, Mannoroc Coven in Desolace, or Serpent’s Coil in the Blasted Lands. These adventures might make it clear that the Burning Legion isn’t just a past threat with lingering echoes in the world—it is a malignant force eagerly awaiting its next opportunity to destroy Azeroth. Worst of all, too many inhabitants of Azeroth seem willing to cooperate with the Legion in bringing about the destruction of their world.

Levels 11–16. The characters learn—perhaps while dealing with satyrs in @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowDiremaul00000]{Dire Maul}, detailed later in this chapter—that a @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze.JournalEntryPage.m7WElR3fFm7BX6eS]{doomguard} has discovered a way to open a portal that will allow the Burning Legion to launch a new invasion of Azeroth. The demon might be reopening the Dark Portal, opening a portal to Argus, or creating a new pathway to another demon-infested world or plane of existence. Perhaps an artifact falls into the adventurers’s hands and the characters fail to prevent the doomguard from using it, or perhaps the characters—intentionally or accidentally—use it themselves. Or perhaps the artifact is a ruse distracting the characters from the real plan to open the portal.

Levels 17–20. An advance force of the Burning Legion storms through the newly opened portal, and the characters face demons of such power and in such numbers as to challenge even their mighty capabilities. At Khadgar’s suggestion, the characters might enter Karazhan to learn how to battle the Legion. In a climactic battle, they beat the Legion back to the portal, preventing any more demons from entering Azeroth.

Endgame. After fighting the Legion back to the portal, the characters pass through the portal themselves! In a realm crawling with demons, they confront ever more powerful commanders of the Burning Legion until they encounter the leader responsible for this incursion, which might be Sargeras (@UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.content.JournalEntry.mmMonstersAtoZ00.JournalEntryPage.SVS7eSxC7Np7xFqi]{Empyrean} with the Fiend creature type).

Dragonflights.name: Dragonflights
Dragonflights.text:
@Embed[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowArtHandouts00.JournalEntryPage.l0biGMf9Vr3zsgZK classes="noborder"]

In the primordial past of Azeroth, five mighty proto-dragons helped the keeper Tyr battle a horrific monster of their kind, the enormous Galakrond. To reward them for their aid, Tyr and most of the other keepers imbued these five with mighty powers so they could safeguard Azeroth. These were the original Dragon Aspects. The keepers also magically altered hundreds of proto-dragon eggs so the creatures that emerged from them would be born in the image of the Aspects. The dragons born from these eggs formed five distinct flights, each serving a different Aspect.

Dragon Aspects

The Dragon Aspects and their flights are described below, including recent changes among the Aspects.

Alexstrasza, the Life-Binder. Alexstrasza and the red dragonflight steward Azeroth’s @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze.JournalEntryPage.DmsSoir1i1hgTyRj]{Red Dragonflight}living creatures. Due to her supreme wisdom and limitless compassion for all living things, Alexstrasza was crowned the Dragonqueen and given dominion over her kind.

Malygos, the Spell-Weaver. Malygos and the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze.JournalEntryPage.g0t7ZVVSG0Vr7TGr]{blue dragonflight} were charged to explore, share, and protect the limitless realms of magic and hidden arcana. During the War of the Ancients, Deathwing slew most of the blue dragonflight, and Malygos spent millennia consumed with grief. During the war against the Lich King, Malygos and the resurgent remnant of the blue dragonflight launched an all-out war against the mortal mages he blamed for the world’s troubles. Kalecgos has since taken on the Spell-Weaver’s mantle.

Neltharion, the Earth-Warder. Neltharion and the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze.JournalEntryPage.jnGTp7LiVzQO8DTY]{black dragonflight} were given charge over the mountains and the deep caverns of the earth. During the War of the Ancients, Neltharion convinced his fellow Aspects to sacrifice a portion of their power and infuse it into the Dragon Soul, an artifact he designed to scour the Burning Legion from Azeroth. But unbeknownst to the other Aspects, Neltharion had fallen prey to the whispers of the @UUID[.QX2LRHkL98AMmC55]{Old Gods}, and he turned the power of the Dragon Soul against his mortal and dragon allies, slaughtering almost the entire blue dragonflight. From that point on, Neltharion was known as Deathwing, and the black dragonflight retreated into a life of fear and seclusion as its members were hunted to the brink of extinction to avenge their Aspect’s betrayal. After the reawakening of the Dragon Isles, Ebyssian became the new Earth-Warder, working to purify the black dragonflight of the Old Gods’ corruption and help its members atone for their misdeeds.

Nozdormu, the Timeless One. Nozdormu and the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze.JournalEntryPage.TzC2d1YrqOCcuCk4]{bronze dragonflight} hold mastery over time itself. They move freely along the timeways, observing the timeways’ flow and ensuring that nothing alters the true timeline.

Ysera, the Awakened. Ysera and the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze.JournalEntryPage.wWBP2j6xQk2Tc6AZ]{green dragonflight} were charged with watching over the growing wilds of Azeroth from their domain, the Emerald Dream. During the Cataclysm, Ysera awakened from her endless dream and now dwells in Ardenweald in the Shadowlands, while her daughter, Merithra, has taken her place as the Green Aspect.

New Aspect. In addition to the recent changes in the leadership of the blue, black, and green dragonflights, a sixth Dragon Aspect has arisen: Vyranoth, called the Frozenheart. The Aspect of Storms represents the Netherwing dragonflight and the Thorignir storm dragons of the Broken Isles in the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowValdrakkenAcc]{Valdrakken Accord}.

Dragon Stat Blocks

Stat blocks for dragons of the five original dragonflights appear in @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze]{chapter 7}. Use the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.content.JournalEntry.mmAppendixBMonst.JournalEntryPage.kZkCXR4ER3nFdmJu#dragons,-chromatic]{chromatic dragons} in the Monster Manual for the proto-dragons in North­rend, in the Dragon Isles, and elsewhere, though most of them are Neutral.

Goals of the Dragonflights

The Dragon Aspects and their dragonflights are complicated and powerful forces on Azeroth. The dragons watch over Azeroth and protect it from other threats discussed in this chapter, particularly the Burning Legion. However, individual dragons and even entire dragonflights have been corrupted or otherwise swayed from their protective missions:

Black Dragonflight. Neltharion and the black dragonflight fell under the influence of the Old Gods and betrayed the other flights. Much later, Deathwing allied with Ragnaros the Firelord under the Old Gods’ influence to bring about the Cataclysm.

Blue Dragonflight. Malygos turned against mortal mages instead of fostering their study of arcane secrets. Other dragons of the blue flight have opposed mortals seeking magical secrets the dragons deemed too dangerous for them to wield, as when Azuregos and his dragonspawn guarded the Highborne relics in the ruins of Eldarath in Azshara.

Bronze Dragonflight. Some bronze dragons have been corrupted by Old Gods or other forces and sought to alter the timeways.

Green Dragonflight. Some green dragons were corrupted by the Emerald Nightmare—the Old Gods’ version of the Emerald Dream. They were known as the nightmare dragonflight. Several of them escaped into Azeroth to spread madness and terror throughout the mortal realms.

Red Dragonflight. During the Second War, an orc warlock used Deathwing’s Dragon Soul, which he renamed the Demon Soul, to enslave Alexstrasza and a number of her flight. The red dragons were forced to serve as war mounts for the Old Horde.

Ahn’Qiraj. Three dragons—a red, a green, and a blue—were imprisoned by the Old God C’Thun in the temple of Ahn’Qiraj.

Of all the dragonflights, the black flight is the most likely to drive conflicts in an Azeroth campaign, thanks to the pervasive corruption of the Old Gods. The schemes of Deathwing’s brood are far reaching and never ending. Deathwing’s consort, Sintharia, created her own dragonflight in an effort to dominate Azeroth. And two of their children, Nefarian and Onyxia, have schemed against the mortal peoples of Azeroth, using human-seeming visages to sow chaos and distrust. Even Wrathion, one of the few black dragons who remains uncorrupted by the Old Gods, plotted to secure the safety of Azeroth by helping the Alliance eliminate the Horde. This pattern might soon change, though, as the black dragons have all but purged the Old Gods’ corruption from their midst in recent years.

A Dragonflights Arc

In a campaign featuring the dragonflights, a dragon most likely serves as a patron for the characters, potentially establishing a relationship that will last for the adventurers’ entire careers. The nature of the dragon patron can shape the campaign:

Bronze Dragon. A bronze dragon such as Chromie (Chronormu) might invite the characters to undertake timewalking quests to experience various points in Azeroth’s history. Later, when they have proved themselves capable, the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze.JournalEntryPage.TzC2d1YrqOCcuCk4]{bronze dragonflight} could rely on them to stave off some force that is trying to alter the true timeline of Azeroth.

Dragon Aspect. A benevolent but mysterious Dragon Aspect such as Alexstrasza or Ysera, seeing low-level adventurers’ potential, might send them on quests that foreshadow conflicts and threats they will face later in their careers.

In World of Warcraft, many conflicts have revolved around the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze.JournalEntryPage.jnGTp7LiVzQO8DTY]{black dragonflight}. This outline sketches a campaign centered on the corruption and redemption of the black dragons, largely inspired by the events of the Dragonflight expansion.

Levels 1–4. A black dragon such as Ebyssian (appearing as the Highmountain tauren spiritwalker Ebonhorn) or Wrathion the Black Prince (in his human visage) serves as patron to the characters as they deal with the weakest minions of the Old Gods, such as @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze.JournalEntryPage.Tog74lVhgL5a8Jo6]{naga} in Darkshore. The patron’s draconic nature might be a secret at this point, or the patron might be open about their desire to redeem the black dragonflight.

Levels 5–10. The adventurers’ patron sends them to investigate reports of @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze.JournalEntryPage.8KLmXbBimVfIpvDV]{black dragon whelps} terrorizing a mountainous region after recent volcanic activity. After the characters deal with a few of the whelps, they spot a @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze.JournalEntryPage.CMHFkaTHLGzQVtJ2]{drake} or two. Their patron asks the characters to determine whether the drakes are guarding a broodmother who could pose a severe threat to the region, but also urges them to avoid combat with the drakes, let alone a full-grown dragon!

Levels 11–16. Another would-be patron contacts the adventurers and causes them to question the true identity of their patron, dropping hints that the patron isn’t what they appear to be. However, this new character is a disguised black dragon—perhaps even Onyxia or Nefarian—who wishes to foil the patron’s plans. Meanwhile, the characters gather help and ultimately battle the broodmother and her guardian drakes.

Levels 17–20. The characters might venture into Blackrock Mountain to confront Nefarian or into Dustwallow Marsh to face Onyxia (see @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowOnyxiasLair00]{Onyxia’s Lair} later in this chapter), serving their patron’s goal of purging corruption from the black dragonflight. Their patron might join the battle alongside them, finally revealing themself as a black drake. The mission complete, the patron invites the characters to Wyrmrest Temple in North­rend to meet the Dragon Aspects and celebrate their victory.

Endgame. Having proved their power and valor, the characters might continue their adventures in service to the Dragon Aspects. They might deal with the dragons in the Nexus or help the Aspects against Deathwing when he rises in the Cataclysm.

Elemental Lords.name: Elemental Lords
Elemental Lords.text:
The elemental lords are the rulers of the primordial elements of air, earth, fire, and water. Forces of chaos and conflict, these elemental powers have been sequestered away in the Elemental Plane for millennia, but their cultists—and the cultists of the @UUID[.QX2LRHkL98AMmC55]{Old Gods}, whom the elemental lords have often served—spread chaos across Azeroth in their name.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowArtHandouts00.JournalEntryPage.fopDBWXCmq8w1fW5 classes="noborder"]

History of the Elemental Lords

Before the titans brought order to Azeroth, the world was ruled by destructive elemental spirits in a constant state of war with one another. For countless millennia, the four elemental lords and their subjects battled for dominance over the primordial world. Al’Akir the Windlord sent his minions to spy on his enemies and sow distrust to weaken them. Neptulon the Tidehunter fought strategically, playing his enemies off against one another before crushing their weakened forces. Ragnaros the Firelord used brute force to boil the seas, melt mountains to slag, and choke the skies with ash. Therazane the Stonemother barricaded herself behind towering mountain ranges, waiting for her enemies to exhaust themselves before emerging to crush them.

Arrival of the Old Gods. When the Old Gods came to Azeroth, the elemental lords joined forces to fight them, but even these mighty beings couldn’t stand against the endless tides of the Old Gods’ minions—the faceless n’raqi and the insectile aqir. Eventually, the Old Gods subjugated the elemental lords, and armies of elemental spirits spread the Old Gods’ Black Empire across the world. The elemental lords were enslaved by the Old Gods and served as their lieutenants across the Black Empire.

Imprisonment by the Pantheon. When the titan-­forged armies of the Pantheon came to order the world, led by the godlike keepers, they imprisoned the elemental lords and their armies in the Elemental Plane, sealed the Old Gods deep beneath the surface of Azeroth, and shattered the Black Empire. Even in their exile, the chaotic elemental lords battled one another for thousands of years. During this long Elemental Sundering, Ragnaros the Firelord feasted on the essence of a mighty air elemental, Thunderaan the Prince of Air. Thunderaan’s remaining essence was stored within a talisman, which Ragnaros broke in two and gave to his two most trusted lieutenants.

War of the Three Hammers. During the War of the Three Hammers, Sorcerer-Thane Thaurissan of the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowDwarf00000000.JournalEntryPage.Ctzza0M3S3xta3Gv]{Dark Iron dwarves} accidentally summoned @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze.JournalEntryPage.hKjF6BYRWJKUDe4p]{Ragnaros} from the Elemental Plane to the Redridge Mountains. Ragnaros’s entry into the world scarred the surrounding area, creating the Burning Steppes and the Searing Gorge. Ragnaros took up residence in Blackrock Mountain and enslaved the Dark Iron dwarves. Only the Firelord’s struggle against the black dragon Nefarian for control of the mountain’s vast caverns and halls kept Ragnaros from becoming a greater threat to the world during the next few centuries. Meanwhile, Neptulon used elemental lieutenants and mortal pawns to strike against Ragnaros and his elementals on Azeroth.

Alliance with Deathwing. After attempting to destroy the other dragonflights during the Second War, the black dragon Deathwing retreated to Deepholm (the earth region of the Elemental Plane) to recuperate and plan his next efforts. When he emerged from Deepholm, he shattered the World Pillar, which kept the Elemental Plane separate from the material world of Azeroth. Parts of the Elemental Plane began to bleed into Azeroth. Deathwing invited the elemental lords to join him in sowing destruction throughout the world, and Ragnaros and Al’Akir gladly accepted. Ragnaros and his fire minions launched an assault on Mount Hyjal to destroy the World Tree Nordrassil, while Al’Akir focused his attention on Uldum, which was the seat of his power under the Black Empire.

Ultimately, adventurers destroyed both Ragnaros and Al’Akir on their home plane, and new elemental lords rose to take their place. Smolderon became the new Firelord, and Thunderaan—resurrected by the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowEarthenRing00]{Earthen Ring}—took on the mantle of Windlord. The shaman of the Earthen Ring marshaled the power of the elemental lords to repel the Burning Legion’s third invasion, but the defeat of the Legion makes it unlikely the elemental lords will ever again have reason to unite with each other, though the Earthen Ring continues to strive for harmony and balance among the four elements.

Stat Blocks

A stat block for @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.actors.Actor.wowRagnarosjY03L]{Ragnaros} appears in chapter 7. For the other elemental lords, use the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmElementalCatac]{Elemental Cataclysm} stat block; choose an appropriate damage type for its Elemental Burst attack, and forgo the random roll for its Cataclysmic Event. The elemental lords are served by the Elementals in the Monster Manual, from mephits to genies, as well as by Humanoid cultists such as @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmCultist0000000]{Cultists}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmCultistFanatic]{Cultist Fanatics}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmElementalCulti]{Elemental Cultists}, and @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmCultistHieroph]{Cultist Hierophants}.

Goals of the Elemental Lords

Given free rein, the elemental lords would return Azeroth to its primordial chaos, in which the primal energy of the four elements would rage uncontrolled and elementals would war constantly against each other for dominion, as they did in ages past. That would be only the first phase of their victory; each elemental lord dreams of then vanquishing the others and transforming Azeroth into a mirror of their own domain of the Elemental Plane.

Of course, the elemental lords haven’t had free rein for countless ages. Even before the Pantheon of Order came to Azeroth, the Old Gods dominated the elemental lords, and the Old Gods still seek to use them. Just before the Cataclysm, N’Zoth ordered the Elemental Lords to fight for the Old Gods in the coming war. When Neptulon and Therazane resisted, N’Zoth’s servants imprisoned Neptulon, and the Twilight’s Hammer cult fought Therazane.

An Elemental Lords Arc

To build a campaign around the elemental lords, you might draw inspiration from the role of the Princes of Elemental Evil in classic D&D adventures. In the same way that Imix and his ilk have been corrupted toward evil by the influence of the Elder Elemental Eye, Ragnaros and the other elemental lords have long been influenced by the Old Gods. You could use Princes of the Apocalypse as a model for a campaign featuring the elemental lords or draw inspiration from the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-dungeon-masters-guide.content.JournalEntry.dmgGreyhawksPrem.JournalEntryPage.6xM2odCqHP4JlcuS]{Elemental Evil} campaign outline in the Dungeon Master’s Guide.

Alternatively, you could build a campaign that focuses on the rivalries between the elemental lords as they lash out in destructive fury against the titan-ordered world. Such a campaign might follow this outline.

Levels 1–4. A shaman—pretending to be a benevolent member of the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowEarthenRing00]{Earthen Ring}—asks the adventurers to investigate what’s happening in Ragefire Chasm. A cult devoted to the Firelord has taken up residence in the chasm and plans to swallow Orgrimmar in lava and ash. On emerging from the chasm, they find their patron has disappeared, and the Earthen Ring denies any knowledge of the quest, even while acknowledging that the fire cult needed to be stopped.

Levels 5–10. Several elders of the Earthen Ring—who seek to persuade the characters that they do actually represent the Earthen Ring, unlike the characters’ last patron—ask the characters to look into a conflict among the centaur tribes in Desolace. The Galak centaur tribe (which serves Al’Akir) is mustering terrible storm magic to assail a new centaur group, drawn from different tribes, that is devoted to Therazane the Stonemother. The Earthen Ring is perplexed at the rise of this cult of Therazane and its ability to unite disparate centaur tribes.

Levels 11–16. Destructive cults of all four elements begin a simultaneous attack against settlements across Azeroth—and against each other. While @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze.JournalEntryPage.Tog74lVhgL5a8Jo6]{naga} cultists of Neptulon assault coastal settlements, air elementals rain down terror from the skies. Earth and fire cultists alike pour out of the earth in volcanic regions to bring havoc to the settled world. The adventurers can’t deal with all the attacks at once, and at least one of the cults gains a significant foothold. In the midst of this assault, the characters might also venture into Maraudon (in Desolace) and confront the elemental forces there.

Levels 17–20. Whichever cult has gained a foothold in the world summons its elemental lord patron into the world. The adventurers must venture into the cult’s stronghold and banish the elemental lord back to the Elemental Plane before the triumphant elemental rampages across the world.

Endgame. After banishing the elemental lord from Azeroth, the adventurers might need to journey to the Elemental Plane to face the elemental lords on their home ground.

Old Gods.name: Old Gods
Old Gods.text:
@Embed[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowArtHandouts00.JournalEntryPage.8U9TImIShS4916LP classes="noborder"]

When the elemental lords warred across the face of primordial Azeroth, eldritch beings of the Void called void lords sought to harness the power of the titans to serve their nihilistic ends. The titans proved incorruptible, so the void lords resorted to trying to find and subvert a slumbering Worldsoul—an entity that would one day become a titan but hadn’t yet manifested its full power. They sent parasitic entities out across the universe to attach themselves to many different worlds, hoping to find a young Worldsoul they could corrupt. Four of these parasitic entities—immense mountains of flesh, eyes, tentacles, and mouths—landed on Azeroth and implanted themselves in its surface to grow like tumors. They dominated the elemental lords and spread their influence over Azeroth, forming the Black Empire. These beings would become known as the Old Gods:

C’Thun. Resembling an enormous, chitin-plated sac ringed with tentacles, studded with eyeballs, pierced with toothy maws, and topped with a gigantic eye, C’Thun is a force of chaos. The keepers of the Pantheon of Order imprisoned it beneath Ahn’Qiraj, where it was served by the qiraji.

N’Zoth. Called the Corrupter, the Deep One, and the Lord of Ny’alotha, N’Zoth resembles a gigantic octopus with eyes ringing its body and a toothy maw at the top of its head. Its eyes and its maw radiate fiery light. N’Zoth is responsible for the corruption of Neltharion, of Queen Azshara and the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze.JournalEntryPage.Tog74lVhgL5a8Jo6]{naga}, and of the tidesages of @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowHuman00000000.JournalEntryPage.b5Jfulr9rBcvQYN9]{Kul Tiras}. The titan-forged keepers imprisoned N’Zoth beneath what would become Nazjatar.

Yogg-Saron. Appearing as a great maw topped with many smaller, tooth-filled maws that almost resemble eyes and surrounded by writhing tangles of tentacles, Yogg-Saron is aptly called the Beast with a Thousand Maws, the God of Death, the Monster in Nightmares, and That Which Must Not Be Named. Imprisoned beneath Ulduar, in what would become North­rend, Yogg-Saron was responsible for initiating the curse of flesh to make titan-forged beings mortal and therefore more corruptible. It also corrupted the World Tree Andrassil and planted a seed of evil within the Emerald Dream, creating the Emerald Nightmare. Its physical essence pervades North­rend in the form of the mineral saronite, which the armies of the Scourge use as fuel, building material, and weaponry.

Y’Shaarj. The so-called God of Seven Heads, Y’Shaarj was said to be the most powerful and wicked of the Old Gods, but it was also the first to be defeated by the Pantheon of Order. The titan Aman’Thul ripped it out of the planet, killing it in the process. Its death did such violence to Azeroth—creating a scar where the life essence of Azeroth spilled out, which became the Well of Eternity and later the Maelstrom—that the keepers imprisoned the other Old Gods rather than destroy them. The keepers sealed the heart of Y’Shaarj beneath the Vale of Eternal Blossoms (in what would become Pandaria), where its dying breath created the seven prime sha—the Sha of Anger, Hatred, Violence, Fear, Doubt, Despair, and Pride.

The minions of the Old Gods include Humanoid cultists (@UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmCultist0000000]{Cultists}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmCultistFanatic]{Cultist Fanatics}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmAberrantCultis]{Aberrant Cultists}, and @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmCultistHieroph]{Cultist Hierophants}), as well as creatures of the Void such as aboleths, mind flayers (known on Azeroth as k’thir, they’re a lesser type of n’raqi or “faceless one”), and several kinds of monsters described in @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze]{chapter 7}: @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze.JournalEntryPage.Tog74lVhgL5a8Jo6]{naga}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze.JournalEntryPage.Bb51wccedduFnY6j]{n’raqi}, and @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze.JournalEntryPage.EHAN3db04nwqzjLq]{voidwalkers}.

Goals of the Old Gods

The Old Gods are responsible for many of the evils that have plagued Azeroth from its earliest days. The void lords sent them to Azeroth to corrupt the Worldsoul at the heart of the planet so it matures into an unstoppable void titan. This possibility was so horrifying to the titan Sargeras that he launched the Burning Crusade to prevent it (see @UUID[.mOeoKWAu3OOx8LP9]{Burning Legion} earlier in this chapter).

Ny’alotha. The dreams of the imprisoned Old Gods created Ny’alotha, the Slumbering City—an alternate reality where the Black Empire had once again conquered Azeroth. When N’Zoth was freed from its imprisonment, it sought to tear down the boundaries between Azeroth and Ny’alotha, imposing the Old Gods’ horrific vision of reality onto the existing world and advancing their plot to corrupt Azeroth’s Worldsoul.

Hour of Twilight. An ancient prophecy speaks of the Hour of Twilight, when the Old Gods would reemerge to end all life on Azeroth. The titans and keepers, glimpsing this possibility, empowered the @UUID[.2MFeGdKlqPZz0K4s]{dragonflights} to fight the minions of the Old Gods and prevent the Hour of Twilight, but the Old Gods’ corruption of Neltharion, the black Dragon Aspect, nearly brought about the end of the world in the Cataclysm. For many years, the Twilight’s Hammer cult has schemed to bring about the Hour of Twilight.

An Old Gods Arc

Antagonists devoted to the Old Gods can be found across the world and at every level of play, and the World of Warcraft game features abundant quests involving such antagonists. A campaign featuring the Old Gods and their servants might unfold according to this outline.

Levels 1–4. The characters might encounter Twilight’s Hammer cultists in Cliffspring Falls and Master’s Glaive in Darkshore, Mo’grosh ogres in Loch Modan, or doomsday cultists at Jaggedswine Farm (outside Orgrimmar) or Mirror Lake Orchard (in Elwynn Forest). In these initial encounters, the cultists behave irrationally and spout nonsense about the end of the world.

Levels 5–10. The characters’ investigations might take them to @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBlackfathomDe]{Blackfathom Deeps}, where they directly experience the corrupting influence of the Old Gods. They might also confront the Necrodark in Highmountain as these cultists strive to free Uul’gyneth the Darkness from its bindings.

Levels 11–16. The bizarre proclamations of the end of the world start to seem like accurate visions of impending doom. The characters might confront the satyr Lord Vyletongue in Maraudon (in Desolace), uncover the corruption of House Stormsong and the tidesages in Stormsong Valley (in Kul Tiras), or face corrupted furbolgs at Vordrassil in the Grizzly Hills (in North­rend). And word might come from Silithus that the Old God C’Thun is stirring in Ahn’Qiraj. At this level, they might face powerful minions of the Old Gods such as @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze.JournalEntryPage.Bb51wccedduFnY6j]{n’raqi}.

Levels 17–20. One of the imprisoned Old Gods begins to break free and extend its malignant power into the world. The characters might venture into the Temple of Ahn’Qiraj to face C’Thun. In addition, they could fight Yogg-Saron’s n’raqi champion in @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowAzjolnerub000]{Azjol-Nerub} or battle corrupted twilight dragons in the Twilight Highlands.

Endgame. After the defeat of C’Thun, N’Zoth tears down the walls of reality that separate Azeroth from Ny’alotha, the Slumbering City. The characters might battle versions of all the Old Gods across their dream re-creation of the nightmarish Black Empire.

Scourge.name: Scourge
Scourge.text:
The Scourge is the result of foul necromantic magic unleashed on the peoples of Azeroth to pave the way for the second invasion of the Burning Legion.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowArtHandouts00.JournalEntryPage.lu0NIr4c80xldgOh classes="noborder"]

History of the Scourge

The demon lord Kil’jaeden forced the first Lich King, the orc shaman Ner’zhul, to create the plague of undeath. The plague spread across North­rend and then into the human lands of Lordaeron, slowly killing those afflicted and then reanimating them as undead under the Lich King’s control. The result was a massive army of skeletons, zombies, ghouls, wraiths, abominations (described in @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowBestiaryOfAze]{chapter 7}), and other undead creatures, supported by living cultists and sinister plague-spreading devices. This horrifying force carved a swath of destruction into Quel’Thalas and used the power of the Sunwell to transform the necromancer Kel’Thuzad into a lich. The devastation of this attack led the survivors of Quel’Thalas to take on the name @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowElf0000000000.JournalEntryPage.aobPGJElQvOcdSnH]{blood elves}.

Rise of Arthas. Ner’zhul chafed against the demons of the Legion and sought to escape from their domination. To that end, he manipulated Arthas Menethil into slaying the nathrezim Mal’Ganis, then lured Arthas to become a death knight and the Lich King’s greatest lieutenant. Eventually, Arthas used the runeblade @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.items.Item.wowFrostmourneKA]{Frostmourne} to shatter the Lich King’s Frozen Throne and free the essence of Ner’zhul from his prison. Arthas absorbed the spirit and became the new Lich King—far more powerful than the first.

After this merging, the new Lich King slept atop the Frozen Throne for several years. While he dreamed and schemed, his minions rebuilt his fortifications at Icecrown Citadel. Finally, the Lich King awakened—having entirely consumed Ner’zhul’s essence—and launched a three-pronged assault on Orgrimmar, Stormwind City, and Theramore, while personally leading his forces against the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowArgentDawn000]{Argent Dawn} forces in the Plaguelands. In retaliation, both the Alliance and the Horde sent forces and champions to North­rend to dismantle the Scourge at its heart.

Bolvar Fordragon’s Sacrifice. As the Lich King faced defeat, however, the spirit of King Terenas Menethil II—freed from Frostmourne to aid the Lich King’s enemies—warned that the Scourge would be more dangerous to the world without a leader than it was under the Lich King’s control. In a noble act of self-sacrifice, Bolvar Fordragon—an Alliance commander and former regent of Stormwind—donned the Lich King’s @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.items.Item.wowHelmofDominAS]{Helm of Domination}, taking command of the Scourge but damning himself to imprisonment in the Frozen Throne. The new Lich King slowly began reining in the terrors of the Scourge.

Years later, the Banshee Queen Sylvanas Windrunner defeated the Lich King and sundered his crown, forever freeing the Scourge from a Lich King’s command. While the masterless Scourge proved a great threat, as the spirit had warned, Bolvar Fordragon had diminished that threat significantly during his reign on the Frozen Throne. To this day, the Scourge remains a danger, but one without clear purpose or direction.

Goals of the Scourge

The goals of the Scourge changed with its varying leadership over the years.

Lich King Ner’zhul. Under Lich King Ner’zhul, the Scourge was a puppet of the @UUID[.mOeoKWAu3OOx8LP9]{Burning Legion} and shared the Legion’s ultimate goal: to purge Azeroth of life so creation can begin again without its fatal flaw.

Lich King Arthas. As Lich King, Arthas continued to serve the Burning Legion but also sought to justify his own deeds. His simultaneous attacks against Orgrimmar and Stormwind City were intended to draw the greatest heroes of both the Horde and the Alliance to North­rend, where he would make them face challenges to weed out the weak and make the strong question their morality just as he had done, planning to raise the mightiest of them as undead lieutenants of the Scourge in a mirror of his journey.

Cult of the Damned. Members of the Cult of the Damned are living servants of the Lich King (including @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmCultist0000000]{Cultists}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmCultistFanatic]{Cultist Fanatics}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmDeathCultist00]{Death Cultists}, and @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmCultistHieroph]{Cultist Hierophants}). The archmage Kel’Thuzad (who later became a @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmLich0000000000]{Lich}) formed the cult and still leads it. Vile people who lusted for power were drawn to the cult in hope of immortality, and Kel’Thuzad founded the sinister school of Scholomance to expand the influence of the cult and share the secrets of necromancy. After the fall of Arthas, the Cult of the Damned became independent of the Scourge, spreading undeath in the Plaguelands.

Lich King Bolvar. Bolvar Fordragon’s goal as Lich King was to weaken the Scourge, or at least to keep it contained. However, his efforts were undermined from within by the Cult of the Damned, and pockets of Scourge undead broke free of the Lich King’s control and continued their relentless assault on the living. With the renewed attacks of the Burning Legion, Bolvar mustered the death knights of the Knights of the Ebon Blade to stand against the Legion’s third invasion.

Dreadlords. One of the architects of the plague of undeath was the dreadlord Mal’Ganis. Though dreadlords are affiliated with the Burning Legion and wield the same fel magic as other demons, they are secretly servants of Sire Denathrius, the ruler of Revendreth in the Shadowlands, created to spread the influence of Death within the other forces of the cosmos. The role of Mal’Ganis and other dreadlords in creating and leading the Scourge hints at a sinister purpose beyond simply weakening Azeroth in preparation for a Legion invasion. Rather, the dreadlords sought to channel the Worldsoul of Azeroth itself through Icecrown Citadel and into the Shadowlands so death might reign supreme.

A Scourge Arc

The threat of the Scourge might unfold in a campaign according to this outline, assuming Arthas still sits on the Frozen Throne.

Levels 1–4. Low-level characters might encounter the Scourge in places such as the Ghostlands and Silverpine Forest—terrifying remnants of the marauding army that swept across Lordaeron during the Third War. Though they are mindless, these skeletons, zombies, and other weak undead strike terror into the hearts of the living.

Levels 5–10. As the characters battle the Scourge, they might take the fight to Shadowfang Keep (see @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowShadowfangKee]{Shadowfang Keep} later in this chapter). They might also encounter the Scarlet Crusade, whose goals initially seem aligned with their own—except for the zealots’ utter abhorrence for anyone different from themselves. The characters might confront these misguided zealots in the Scarlet Monastery (also described in this chapter).

The characters might also face the Scourge in North­rend, as the characters respond to Arthas’s provocations and confront him on his home turf. This could lead the characters into partnership with the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowArgentDawn000]{Argent Dawn}, who show themselves to be everything the Scarlet Crusade should have been.

Levels 11–16. As the Cult of the Damned becomes more troublesome, the adventurers might venture into Scholomance to put an end to the cult’s vile teachings. In North­rend, they might face the Scourge and minions of the Old Gods in @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.book.JournalEntry.wowAzjolnerub000]{Azjol-Nerub}. As they draw closer to the Lich King’s seat of power—perhaps advancing through the Sholazar Basin, the Grizzly Hills, or the Dragonblight—they face ever more powerful minions of the Scourge.

Levels 17–20. The adventurers might confront Kel’Thuzad in Naxxramas before battling the Lich King in Icecrown Citadel. Perhaps the characters will face Bolvar Fordragon’s choice: Will one of them don the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-world-warcraft.items.Item.wowHelmofDominAS]{Helm of Domination} to keep the Scourge subdued, damning themself to the Frozen Throne in the process?

Endgame. After defeating the Lich King, the characters might venture into the Shadowlands to face the dreadlords and Sire Denathrius and finally end the Scourge.
